Title: Extracellular Vesicles in Osteogenesis: A Comprehensive Review of Mechanisms and Therapeutic Potential for Bone Regeneration
Snippet: Regeneration of bone tissue, particularly in large segmental defects or ischemic environments, requires not only robust osteogenesis but also the formation of a well-organized vascular network to support cellular viability and metabolic activity. Vascular endothelial cells (ECs), which line the inner surface of blood vessels, are essential for bone repair through their dual role in initiating and sustaining angiogenesis and coordinating osteogenesis. A principal mechanism by which ECs influence bone healing is the secretion of EVs, including exosomes and microvesicles, collectively termed EC-derived EVs (EC-EVs). These vesicles encapsulate diverse bioactive molecules-proteins, lipids, mRNAs, and miRNAs-that mediate intercellular signaling along the endothelial-osteogenic axis. EC-EVs are increasingly recognized for their ability to couple angiogenesis and osteogenesis, a process critical for the survival, proliferation, and differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells in regenerative bone environments [86]. 

Key angiogenic mediators within EC-EVs include vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), angiopoietin-1 (Ang1), and fibroblast growth factor-2 (FGF2). These molecules drive endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and capillary tube formation, while delivery via EVs ensures spatially restricted and temporally controlled release within the local tissue microenvironment. VEGF, in particular, acts by binding to VEGFR-2 on endothelial cells, triggering downstream phosphorylation cascades that promote angiogenic sprouting and vessel maturation. Concurrently, these factors exert indirect osteogenic effects by establishing a perfused niche favorable for bone matrix deposition and remodeling. The osteoinductive capacity of EC-EVs is further supported by their miRNA cargo, notably miR-126 and miR-210. miR-126 enhances endothelial cell proliferation and tube formation via PI3K/Akt and MAPK/ERK signaling, and also modulates osteogenic marker expression, such as RUNX2 and osteocalcin, in MSCs through paracrine interaction [62].

Title: Exosome-mediated Piezo1 activation in 3D-printed titanium scaffolds promotes repair of femoral head osteonecrosis
Snippet: To elucidate the ability of P-Exos@HAMA/Ti to support both osteogenesis and angiogenesis-two tightly linked processes essential for bone regeneration-we examined BMSCs and rat-derived vascular endothelial cells (VECs) across a seven-group experimental framework. Under osteogenic induction, the readouts displayed a consistent hierarchy across groups (Fig. 4a-d). Ti or HAMA alone produced the weakest ARS and ALP staining, whereas incorporation of exosomes (Exos@HAMA/Ti) markedly enhanced signal intensity. Among Dex-challenged groups, P-Exos@HAMA/Ti exhibited the highest levels, with Yoda1 + Exos showing a comparable enhancement. These phenotypic gains were accompanied by upregulated expression of osteogenic markers-Runx2, Osterix, and OCN-at both protein and mRNA levels, along with a distinct Piezo1 band detected in P-Exos@HAMA/Ti lysates (Fig. 4e-j). 

Immunofluorescence analysis likewise revealed enhanced Piezo1 expression, characterized by a more continuous pericellular and cytoplasmic distribution, stronger nuclear localization of Runx2 and Osterix, and greater extracellular OCN deposition under exosomebearing conditions. These features were supported by a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic intensity ratio for Runx2/ Osterix, more continuous OCN-positive matrices along cell-cell interfaces, and intensified Piezo1 signals. 

Among the groups, P-Exos@HAMA/Ti exhibited the most uniform and pronounced staining patterns, followed by Yoda1 + Exos and Exos@HAMA/Ti, whereas Ti or HAMA alone showed minimal signals. The Normal group provided the upper reference bound (Fig. 4k-n and Fig. S9). This hierarchy mirrored the ALP and ARS outcomes observed under osteogenic induction.
